findings.detail: Measured corpus-wide: 669 seeds contain rows that disagree on spelling, all in the two headword-seeded sources (ngata 537, papakupu 132). They split into two defects with one cause. 492 are balanced spellings — genuine homographs merged into a single seed (ngata manawa 9 / mānawa 6, heart vs mangrove; mata 17 / matā 7; koti 5 / kōti 3, coat vs court). 177 are lopsided 4:1 or worse — a typo'd row poisoning a uniform seed (huri 27 / hūri 1; taka 24 / tāka 1; this cluster 7 / 1). Both follow from grouping on headword_search rather than the headword itself. [RESOLVED in 0713395]
findings.subject: concept_evidence.lexeme_key
findings.summary: One misspelled row vetoes its whole source's attachment. ngata and papakupu seed by headword_search, which is macron-blind, so all eight ngata rows form one seed; the anti-chaining rule then refuses the seed against any concept ANY member blocks, and the single 'ahuaatua' row blocks on macron disagreement. The seven correct rows are isolated with it.

findings.detail: williams:320 is a pure pointer entry — the source printed 'Aranga, n. || ara (ii).' and the content is carried by its see_also, which resolves to williams:302 sense 1998470. The headword strip left 'n.' behind as the definition, and part_of_speech is NULL. Moving it puts the POS where it belongs and stops a sense claiming a gloss it does not have. Only 2 senses corpus-wide are like this (also williams:4145 'Makanga'), so this is a patch rather than a pipeline fix.
findings.subject: williams:320#1
findings.summary: the gloss is the part-of-speech abbreviation 'n.' and nothing else

findings.detail: 'inter.numeral How many?' and 'prefix initial element in a small set of compund words...'. papakupu records POS in sense.part_of_speech for 2,703 senses, so the field exists and these two bypass it. 13 papakupu senses open with a POS abbreviation ('hama' = 'v.t., dislodge, hammer', 'makariri' = 'n., cold', 'koutou' = 'pron. 2nd pers. pl. all of you') - below the threshold where a parser change is cheaper than judging them, so patched here rather than escalated. The POS values are the source's own words, title-cased to papakupu's convention; the source's spelling 'compund' is left as it stands.
findings.subject: papakupu:395#1 ; papakupu:396#1
findings.summary: the part of speech is glued to the front of the gloss

findings.detail: Mechanism: _seed_groups returns seeds sorted, so for this key the order is hepatakakupu, paekupu, te_aka, te_matatiki. paekupu creates the concept; te_aka attaches to paekupu alone (coverage ~0.02 against a 40-word definition, df(galaxy)=15 > ceiling 10, so weak on both axes); te_matatiki then attaches to {paekupu, te_aka} and earns gloss_overlap via te_aka. The evidence rows show it — te_matatiki carries BOTH kinds, te_aka only the weak one. Because concept.confidence is min() over members, te_aka's frozen weak tier makes the whole concept uncertain, so a four-way agreement on 'galaxy' is withheld from the app. This is order-dependence, not a threshold problem: no tuning of COVERAGE_FLOOR or DISTINCT_CEILING fixes a member scored against the wrong partner. The fix direction would be to re-score members against the concept's final membership after formation settles. [RESOLVED in 811c240]
findings.subject: 54_build_concepts.form_concepts
findings.summary: A member's confidence is frozen at the moment it attaches, against whichever members happened to be in the concept then — not against the concept's final membership. te_aka 'galaxy.' and te_matatiki 'Galaxy' score coverage 1.00 against each other, which is ordinary evidence, yet te_aka is tiered uncertain: it attached when only paekupu was present, scored weak against paekupu's encyclopaedic definition, and never got credit for te_matatiki arriving afterwards.

findings.detail: paekupu prints the headword '(Te) Ra Rangaawatea', where the parenthesis marks the article as optional. normalise_search_key keeps the parenthesis, so headword_search is '(te) ra rangawatea' and the cluster is keyed on that. A reader searching the bare term does not reach it. Systemic rather than local: 707 entries hold a parenthetical anywhere in headword_search and 291 begin with one - paekupu 258, te_aka 18, kimikupu_hou 11, te_matatiki 4 - and 1,080 sweep clusters are keyed with a bracket. Not all are the same shape: te_aka's '(ka/he/te) tau/kino (ke) (hoki)' is an idiom whose parentheses mark genuine alternation, and stripping those would be wrong. Deferred rather than queued because a per-cluster patch cannot address it and section 6 records the precedent - a systemic defect belongs in the script that causes it, as D19 and D20 did.
findings.subject: paekupu:rangaawatea-2
findings.summary: an optional article inside headword_search makes the term findable only with it

findings.detail: te_aka prints '[to] tara!', where the square brackets mark an implied possessive. headword_search keeps both the brackets and the exclamation mark, so the cluster is keyed '[to] tara!' and a reader searching the bare word does not reach it. The finding filed on '(te) ra rangawatea' counted round brackets only and reported 707 entries; counting square brackets, exclamation and question marks as well gives 883, across eight sources - paekupu 506, te_aka 252, kimikupu_hou 57, papakupu 28, williams 20, te_matatiki 14, hepatakakupu 4, tregear_exceptions 2. Round brackets alone are 707, square 139, ellipsis 128, slash 48, exclamation 46, question 35. Recorded here rather than re-filing the whole finding per cluster, which is the noise section 4 warns about. Still deferred: the shapes are not all one defect, since te_aka's idiom keys genuinely alternate, and the fix belongs in the key-building script rather than in any cluster.
findings.subject: te_aka:8521
findings.summary: square brackets and terminal punctuation reach headword_search too; the earlier count of 707 was low

findings.detail: '(success)' narrows which English 'coup' is meant — the achievement, not the overthrow. It qualifies the gloss rather than forming part of it, and Paekupu puts the same kind of note in a domain while Te Aka folds it into prose. findings.detail: This entry carries form alt_spelling 'ara - to rise up', which is the component word and its meaning, not a spelling of 'Aranga'. SYSTEMIC and large: paekupu contributes 11,875 of the corpus's form rows and the field holds two other things entirely. 6,519 carry ' - ' and are morpheme glosses ('wete - to release, set free', 'hapara (haparapara) - surgery, operation') — the derivation of a coined term, which is the same shape as Te Matatiki's bracket derivations already routed to cross_ref relations. The other 5,356 are synonyms: 'ahanoa' and 'tuhanga' list each other and are both glossed 'object (computing)'. Nothing in the field is a variant form, so the app's 'this word has variants' signal is almost entirely false. Escalated as a pipeline fix.
findings.subject: paekupu:aranga ; paekupu (all 11,875 alt_spelling rows)
findings.summary: paekupu's alternative_words are not alternative spellings — none of them are

findings.detail: te_aka:21108 is [proper noun - person | Historical Loan Word], glossed 'Adair.', with an example about Mr Adair's steamer between Gisborne and Awanui. It carried ATEA 'clear, free from obstruction', ATEA '(myth.) the last of the Ages' and PN.QAATEA 'Clear, unobstructed'. A borrowed word cannot descend from Proto-Polynesian — inheritance and borrowing are mutually exclusive — so the link is wrong wherever the loan marker is right. SYSTEMIC: 8,314 links reached 2,457 loan-marked entries the same way ('Aki' = Jack <- PN.-QAKI.1, 'Ahua' = Asshur <- NP.AAFUA, 'aaka' = ark, 'aamene' = amen). Fixed in the pipeline as D23 rather than per cluster.
findings.subject: te_aka:21108#1 <- ATEA (tregear) x2, PN.QAATEA (pollex)
findings.summary: three Proto-Polynesian cognate sets were attached to 'Atea', a transliteration of the surname Adair

findings.detail: Williams marks a variant with '=' at the head of an entry, distinct from the '‖' compare marker the parser already extracts into see_also and citation rows. The '=' was never read, so the link was invisible and anything behind it stayed stranded. SYSTEMIC: 680 senses opened with '=' and 611 of those entries had no relation whatsoever — 'Ahine = wahine.', 'Ahore = kahore, ad. Not.', 'Ahau = au, awau, awahau, pron.' findings.detail: 'He kupu mino.' is Maori for 'it is a loan word' — a marker about the entry, not another term for it. D22 routed every non-dashed alternative_words value to a synonym relation, so 411 of them became synonyms whose target is a sentence. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D27: they now populate entry.loan_marker, where Te Aka's marker already lives, which also makes them visible to the D23 etymology filter. 409 paekupu entries gained a loan marker. Some name the source language — (reo Hapanihi) Japanese, (reo Wiwi) French, (reo Itariana) Italian, (reo Hiperu) Hebrew — which is the only place in the corpus a loan's origin language is recorded.
findings.subject: paekupu:hate

findings.detail: te_aka:13131 'heart (playing-card suit)' and te_aka:916 'shirt.' are both [loan, noun | Loan Word, Noun] with loan_marker NULL, while te_aka:22815 'shirt.' and te_aka:22818 'Fate.' in the same cluster carry the marker. findings.subject: te_aka:13131 ; te_aka:916

findings.detail: 'Eng.' says the word is borrowed from English — the same fact Te Aka puts in loan_marker and paekupu in 'he kupu mino'. 90 papakupu glosses carry it. Not patched here: it is a third encoding of the same fact and belongs in the loan-origin model rather than being stripped, since unlike the other two it names the source language.
findings.subject: papakupu:343#1
findings.summary: the gloss opens with an etymology marker, 'Eng. shirt'

findings.detail: Systemic, and measured: same source + same headword + byte-identical gloss_en across different entry ids gives te_aka 1,648 groups over 3,399 entries, ngata 1,096 over 2,419, paekupu 978 over 2,013 — roughly 7,800 entries. williams and papakupu have 13 groups each, so this is concentrated in the three largest modern sources. Each duplicate becomes its own concept because the design trusts a source's entry-per-lexeme structure, so this fragments words the source itself considers one. NOT proposed as a fix here: te_aka legitimately files one transliteration under several entries for different referents (this same cluster has six 'Hene' entries for Shen, John-the-ship, Hen, Jenner, John and Gennys, correctly separate), so identical-gloss duplicates and deliberate referent splits need distinguishing before anything is changed. Examples of the identical-gloss class: Marikena, Moromona, Nōmana, Papita, Wikitōria, each 4 entries with one gloss. [RETRACTED 2026-09-17: the signature was tested and does not hold. te_aka's identical-gloss groups are overwhelmingly DELIBERATE part-of-speech filing, not duplication — Marikena has four entries glossed 'American.' as proper noun - other / adjective / proper noun - person, Wikitoria likewise across person / place / simple noun. The hypothesised signature (exactly one entry carrying POS and examples) fits 33 of 1,648 groups, 2%. There was never a ~7,800-entry defect. What survives is narrow: 53 te_aka groups where a POS-less entry shadows a POS-bearing one with an identical gloss — the shape this finding was first raised on (hene 52415 bare vs 48937 noun+example), plus hapui, horukura, huataue, huitupoko, hurumanu. Two corrections to the original claims: ngata's 1,096 groups are already unified by the macron seeding fix in 0713395, and duplicates do NOT structurally fail to merge — 1,109 concepts hold duplicate entries together, bridged by a shared third-source member.]
findings.subject: te_aka:48937 / te_aka:52415
findings.summary: Two te_aka entries for 'hene', both glossed 'anus.', becoming two separate concepts. 48937 carries a noun POS and an example; 52415 carries neither. One word, filed twice.

findings.detail: The gloss read 'Interrogative numeral. How many?. When used with reference to persons it generally has toko prefixed. Te hia ? which in order? 2. An indefinite number. Several.' - the interrogative and the indefinite quantifier, two different words by the cognate evidence above, in one sense. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D28. williams_senses._sense_spans demanded a strict run from 1, and Williams numbers the first sense only when it needs to, so on 136 entries the run never started. A second cause with the same symptom: the separator class before a marker was [.)], excluding the '?' and '!' that end Maori example sentences - which is precisely why this entry failed, at 'Te hia ? ... 2.'. williams senses 24,555 -> 24,976; embedded markers 235 -> 99. The two indefinite-number examples moved to sense 2 with the split.
findings.subject: williams:1090
findings.summary: two senses were collapsed into one because Williams left the first sense unnumbered

findings.detail: paekupu's kawa is a Putaiao noun 'sour', a Hangarau noun 'protocol', a Hangarau adjective 'sour, bitter' and a Tikanga a-Iwi noun 'protocol'. himoemoe is a Hangarau adjective, so the referent is kawa-3, and subject domain plus part of speech name it without judgement. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D29. resolve_relations_by_domain now narrows same-headword candidates by shared subject domain and breaks a remaining tie on part of speech, resolving 7,070 relations (unresolved 21,746 -> 14,676) across paekupu and He Pataka Kupu. Sources with no domains are untouched. This relation now points at paekupu:kawa-3 'sour, bitter'.
findings.subject: paekupu:himoemoe synonym -> kawa
findings.summary: unresolved because paekupu holds four kawa entries, and the source itself says which one

findings.detail: williams:1252#3 names the three forms of this bird-snare pole - 'hiwi ariki, pou tauru, and kiira' - so 'pou tauru' is a real term, but He Pataka Kupu does not define it and says so by wrapping it. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D30. Measured over the whole source the marker separates almost perfectly: of the wrapped values 728 are not headwords and 6 are, of the plain ones 13,922 are and 4 are not. Checked before acting - stripping the parens and re-matching resolves only 3 of 732, so these are genuinely undefined terms rather than a matching failure. parse_synonym now strips only a balanced outer pair, keeping '(tahi (i te) tahua )' intact and leaving unbalanced text like '(tu atu' alone. 732 relations marked, 5 resolved anyway where the term does have an entry.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:10279#5 synonym -> '(pou tauru )'
findings.summary: the parentheses are a source marker meaning the synonym has no entry, not part of the term

findings.detail: Williams has two entries on key 'ho' - 1255 'Ho' pout/droop/shout, and 1256 'Ho' the compound-forming verb. The see_also resolver's match() ended in cands[0], taking the first entry sharing the key, so hoatu linked to 'pout, droop, shout' and the stored target spelling was overwritten with that entry's headword. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D32. Of 4,533 target matches 2,293 had one candidate and 1,064 were settled by the roman sense; the other 1,176 were decided by list position. Williams lower-cases a cross-reference but keeps its macrons, so spelling is evidence - 'ho' is Ho not Ho-macron, 'kahu' is Kahu not Kahu-macron - which settles 206; for the remaining 970 no link is now made. see_also rows resolved 3,352 -> 2,744, and the fall is the point.
findings.subject: williams:1267 see_also target
findings.summary: the cross-reference pointed at the wrong homograph, and had done so 1,176 times

findings.detail: The 'Put forth' record lists 'hoatu, hoatutia, whakamahoe, whakamahoetia, whakan' and whakan is not a word - Maori words end in a vowel. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D31. Wakareo caps the equivalents run at 50 characters: the longest such list anywhere in the source is exactly 50, and 103 of the lists that reach it end in a consonant. All 103 tails were reviewed individually and not one is a word - 'w', 'wh', 'whak', 'p', 't', 'pur', 'rap'. The damage is upstream in body_raw, so the landing table keeps it; what the unified core must not do is mint an entry for a word the source never asserted. ngata entries 33,878 -> 33,775. A cut landing on a vowel is undetectable and 119 lists reach the cap that way; guessing at those would be inventing.
findings.subject: ngata:WR-HMN.10139#40306~5 'whakan'
findings.summary: a truncated fragment had become an entry with a headword and a synonym relation

findings.detail: POLLEX segments a reflex for the reader, and both bridges split on the '/'. PN.SOI.3 'Interjection expressing exasperation' has the Maori reflex 'Hoi/hoi' - the word is hoihoi - so the set keyed to `hoi` and every entry here inherited it, while the 9 hoihoi entries glossed 'be noisy, deafening, loud' had none. FJ.FOHI 'Remove skin, peel' reached it via 'Hoi/puu', which is hoipuu. TA.MAHOI 'Supernatural being' via 'Tini o te /mahoi/hoi'. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D33. 639 of 3,424 Maori reflexes (19%) contain '/', and the joined form is a real corpus headword in 589. Of the 32 that join to nothing, none is an alternative-form separator - 'Ranga/ia' is glossed by POLLEX itself as 'Passive form of ra(ra)nga'. pollex_entry_links 72,152 -> 57,189. The etymology was being taken off the right word and put on the wrong one, which is D23's failure mode reached through our own parsing rather than the source's.
findings.subject: all 17 hoi entries ; PN.SOI.3 ; FJ.FOHI ; TA.MAHOI
findings.summary: three cognate sets reached this cluster because a morpheme boundary was read as a separator

findings.detail: Each unmacronised sense names 'hōmai' as a synonym - the source itself linking the two lemmas - and all three sat unresolved because He Pātaka Kupu has three hōmai entries and the resolver will not guess. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D34. He Pātaka Kupu is a synonym-set dictionary: one definition serves every headword in the set, verbatim, and 3,763 of its 10,443 definitions are shared by two or more headwords. So a repeated definition names the sense meant. All three now resolve to their sense-matched twin - 17631->17681, 18784->25797, 25798->18753 - which is exactly the pairing the dedup work needs. 3,127 relations resolved corpus-wide; unresolved 15,280 -> 12,153.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:17631 ; 18784 ; 25798 synonym -> 'hōmai'
findings.summary: the source states the duplication and the relation could not be resolved, because three candidates carried the headword

findings.detail: The parser carried an explicit strip - re.sub(r'\s*\(\s*\d+\s*\)\s*', '', part) - that removed the (N) from every synonym, so 'hikoki (2)' became 'hikoki'. Since a sense is a row in this source, that pointer identifies one entry outright rather than merely narrowing it, which is the difference between a reference that resolves and one that joins the sweep's queue. Fixed as part of D35; 1,741 pointers recovered. Worth noting the parser's own helper _text_no_sup is documented as skipping 'sense-ref numbers', so the convention was understood and the <sup> - which is the target's homograph index, not its sense - is correctly still dropped.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu synonym sense pointers
findings.summary: a synonym naming one sense of its target arrived naming none

findings.detail: hepatakakupu:300 lists turori twice among its synonyms, and both turori rows carry a definition byte-identical to hurori's. Chasing that into sources/hepataka/raw/9889.html found the reason: turori sense 1 carries hurori (1) - word 1226 IS hurori - so the definition is identical because it is the same definition, quoted. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D35. 14,379 of these links exist across 8,836 of the 14,996 saved pages. This is canonical-entry data addressed by id rather than by spelling, which is what the concept layer has been missing, and it was on disk the whole time. 14,370 relations emitted and 14,340 resolved to a specific SENSE (99.8%), because He Pataka Kupu splits every sense into its own row so (word_id, sense_number) names exactly one entry.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:303 'turori' ; hepatakakupu:300 'hurori'
findings.summary: the source names the entry holding each sense's master definition, and we were reading none of it

findings.detail: It is a definition in a gloss column, and it actively harms matching: a 40-word gloss gives every partner a near-zero Jaccard coverage, so paekupu can essentially only ever attach on the distinctiveness axis. That is likely why paekupu's cross-source reach is 26.7%, low for a source with 16,486 senses. Worth measuring how many paekupu glosses are definition-length before deciding anything. [ANSWERED 2026-09-17: the hypothesis behind this finding — that definition-length gloss_en depresses paekupu's cross-source reach — is FALSIFIED. Gloss length does not predict reach: temarareo has the longest glosses in the corpus (mean 6.2 content words, 17.7% at >=10) and reaches 79.8%; papakupu matches paekupu's lengths almost exactly (mean 5.0 vs 4.8) and reaches 55.7% against paekupu's 28.7%. The actual cause is vocabulary, not glossing: only 45.6% of paekupu's 16,486 entries share a headword key with ANY other source, the lowest in the corpus, because it is a coinage dictionary and over half its words do not exist elsewhere to be matched. Normalised against what is reachable at all it sits at 63%, below ngata 85%, williams 80% and te_aka 79% but unremarkable. The long gloss remains a field_placement observation — a 40-word encyclopaedic definition is not a gloss — but it is not the cause of anything measurable, so there is no pipeline fix here.]
findings.subject: paekupu:ikarangi

findings.detail: itinga is iti + -nga, and Williams printed it under Itaupa - the preceding headword on page 80, not its base. A first cut of D36 recorded 1,875 parents of which 308 (16%) were this: atawhai from atatuhi, haepapa from haeoratu, hangahanga from 'Hanga kino'. Recording those asserts a derivation that does not exist, which the rubric forbids outright. supported_parents now requires the parent's key to appear inside the child's, and itinga records nothing. Worth keeping as the case that shows parent_headword means 'printed under', not 'derived from' - a distinction that would have quietly corrupted 308 rows.

findings.detail: williams:1185301 'itinga' has kind='sub' and parent_headword='Itaupa' in the parsed JSON, and williams_entries had no column for it, so 3,032 recorded derivations never reached the database. SYSTEMIC; fixed as D36. 2,801 of the 2,956 sub-headwords contain their parent's key outright - whakaae from Ae, akahukahu from Akahu, muanga from Mua - which is what a Maori derivative looks like by prefix, suffix or reduplication. 1,507 derived_from relations now recorded, all resolved to an entry. This is WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN's step 1 for Williams: attested, already resolved, no new claims.
findings.subject: williams:1185301 'itinga' ; the 3,032 Williams sub-entries

findings.detail: Both duplicates found so far have the same signature: the lower-numbered entry carries POS and examples, the 5xxxx-numbered one carries neither and repeats the gloss verbatim. That is a sharper discriminator than 'identical gloss' alone and would separate these from te_aka's deliberate referent splits (six 'Hene' entries for six different people and a ship). Worth testing against the 1,648 te_aka duplicate groups before anything is changed. [RETRACTED 2026-09-17: the signature was tested and does not hold. te_aka's identical-gloss groups are overwhelmingly DELIBERATE part-of-speech filing, not duplication — Marikena has four entries glossed 'American.' as proper noun - other / adjective / proper noun - person, Wikitoria likewise across person / place / simple noun. The hypothesised signature (exactly one entry carrying POS and examples) fits 33 of 1,648 groups, 2%. There was never a ~7,800-entry defect. What survives is narrow: 53 te_aka groups where a POS-less entry shadows a POS-bearing one with an identical gloss — the shape this finding was first raised on (hene 52415 bare vs 48937 noun+example), plus hapui, horukura, huataue, huitupoko, hurumanu. Two corrections to the original claims: ngata's 1,096 groups are already unified by the macron seeding fix in 0713395, and duplicates do NOT structurally fail to merge — 1,109 concepts hold duplicate entries together, bridged by a shared third-source member.]
findings.subject: te_aka:49068 / te_aka:52544

findings.subject: williams:378#1

findings.detail: Both 'Sense' entries headword as macronised aronga; ngata's own 'Direction', 'Drift', 'Facet', 'Aspect' and 'Mean' entries headword as plain aronga. Every other source in the cluster is unmacronised — te_aka:424, paekupu (three entries), williams:378 and williams:1036001, hepatakakupu, kimikupu_hou. te_aka:424#3 glosses 'sense, separate meaning (of a word, phrase or sentence)' unmacronised, which is exactly what ngata macronises. The disagreement is within ngata as much as across sources, so it reads as an error rather than a variant. Recorded only: per D18 a macron cannot be inherited on search-key identity alone without risking a homograph merge, and the concept layer is what licenses it.
findings.subject: ngata:WR-HMN.11455#42278~1 ; ngata:WR-HMN.11455#42279~1

findings.subject: ngata:WR-HMN.7322#36204~2#1

Te Aka writes the distinction consistently and marks the loan. Recorded so the identity pass never groups them: this is the case where a macron carries the whole difference, and merging on search-key identity would put an English surname inside a Maori concept.
findings.subject: te_aka:21108 'Atea' vs te_aka:478 / 49679 'ātea'

findings.subject: te_aka:22001#1

Separately, te_aka:22197 'ham.' and te_aka:22198 'jam.' are two DIFFERENT English words transliterated to the same Maori form, both marked Historical Loan Word. Their examples are price-list fragments ('Hamu ... 0 1 0 te pauna', '... 150 pauna hamu...'), which is itself good evidence of a borrowing rather than an inherited word.
findings.subject: te_aka:22197 ; te_aka:22198

findings.detail: 'haate' is both 'shirt' (hepatakakupu, ngata, paekupu, papakupu, taikupu, te_aka x2) and 'heart', the playing-card suit (ngata, te_aka:13131). 'Hate' unmacronised is 'Fate', the island — a place name. Every sense in this cluster is a borrowing; there is no inherited Maori word here at all, which is why the cluster carries no etymology and correctly should not.
findings.subject: te_aka:22818 'Hate' vs the 'haate' entries
findings.summary: three unrelated English words share this Maori spelling, and one is distinguished only by the macron

findings.detail: Measured: te_aka x paekupu cov 0.40 df 11 (weak, by 0.10 and by 1); te_aka x williams cov 0.20 df 115 (weak, decisively); paekupu x williams cov exactly 0.50 (ordinary, rescued by the inclusive boundary). At DISTINCT_CEILING 20 — the provisional value before the grid search — te_aka x paekupu would have attached as ordinary and the concept would have shipped. The tightening from 20 to 10 is what withheld it. That ceiling was set at 10 rather than the measured cliff of 7 to buy clearance against corpus drift; this cluster is one concrete cost of that choice, and is exactly the labelled evidence the re-tuning mechanism in the design's §6 was built to accumulate. One data point argues for nothing on its own — it is recorded so a re-tune has it.
findings.subject: concept 664676
findings.summary: Correct grouping, tiered uncertain, would not have shipped. All three sources gloss haukāinga as home / home people and plainly belong together. The concept is uncertain only because min() takes the weakest member, and te_aka's attachment misses BOTH axes narrowly: coverage 0.40 against a floor of 0.50, distinctiveness 11 against a ceiling of 10.

findings.detail: Recorded to count recurrences. Two clusters judged, two instances: it is not rare. See the isolation table in the gloss-evidence spec §7.

'Te wāhi o te tinana e puta ai ngā para mārō o te arakai' is the anus — the same word as te_aka:48937 and williams:1056 — but with no gloss_en there is no evidence kind that can reach it, so it sits alone.

findings.detail: 'Pennantia corymbosa, a tree. = kaikomako (Po.).', '... = tanekaha.', '... = akerautangi.' D24 extracts the marker only at the head of a definition, on the grounds that a '=' later in the text is a gloss equivalence belonging to the prose. These samples suggest some mid-text ones are entry-level equivalences after all, with '(Po.)' marking a dialect. Recorded as a candidate rather than acted on: distinguishing the two readings is judgement, and widening D24 on a guess would undo a scope decision that was made deliberately.
findings.subject: williams glosses containing a mid-text '= target'
findings.summary: 1,800 glosses carry an equals reference that D24 deliberately left in place

findings.detail: Interrogative numeral 'how many?'; indefinite quantifier 'several, many'; desiderative prefix hia- (hiakai, hiamoe); the exclamatory hia of williams:1092; hiia 'draw', properly hiia and a form of hii; and four unrelated loans - te_aka:23536 'share?' (the source's own query), 23537 'Sia', 23539 'Lear', 23540 'Sir'. The four loans correctly carry no etymology, which is D23/D26 working. A concept layer must not treat this key as one concept, and a macronisation pass must not touch it: hia and hiia are genuinely different words here.
findings.subject: the hia cluster as a whole
findings.summary: nine entries on this key are at least seven unrelated words

findings.detail: 'From Austronesian *“ulu head, P-Polynesian *‘ulu head, hair + P-Polynesian kefu light coloured...', 'From the same source as unu 2; cf. Hawaiian, Tongan unuhi “take out, withdraw”', 'No examples in database, linked to upoko', 'Meremere Penfold, March 2003', 'Cf. Ngai, Ngare'. Alongside these, ordinary case and spelling variance - 'Demonstrative determiner' three ways, 'Defintive', 'Dervived noun', 'Auxilliary'. The etymology strings are genuine content in the wrong field and the attributions are editorial metadata; both are recoverable. Recorded rather than acted on because normalising this vocabulary is the canonical-POS-list work the user scoped separately, and it should be done once across all sources, not per cluster.
findings.subject: papakupu sense.part_of_speech vocabulary

findings.detail: williams:1092#1 ends 'Used to express surprise and admiration. (What difficulty you must have had in coming through on the high tide!).' - the translation of its own first example, which was extracted without a citation. 663 williams senses end in a long parenthetical and 120 of those have an uncited first example. But sampling shows they are not one defect: 'Begin to wane, of the moon (?become crescent-shaped).' and 'Curved (applied to the waning moon).' are legitimate gloss qualifiers; 'Ebb. (Rotorua oral tradition texts)' is a stranded citation; 'Earthworm. hei toketoke hi tuna (Nga Moteatea 70).' is a stranded Maori example with its citation. Separating them requires deciding what each parenthetical is, which is judgement. Same boundary reached at 'herepu' - the mechanically separable seam in Williams is close to exhausted.
findings.subject: williams glosses ending in a parenthetical
findings.summary: 120 look like a stranded example translation, but the shape has at least three causes

findings.detail: Three clusters judged, three instances. Counting recurrences rather than re-measuring; see the isolation table in the gloss-evidence spec §7.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:2220 / 2226

findings.detail: 2,158 paekupu headword keys carry more than one entry, 4,911 entries in all, and on 976 of those keys two entries share an identical English gloss - 'aho tuaiwi' / 'spinal cord' twice, '(katu) noho haukori' / 'active lifestyle' twice. Checked rather than assumed: the pairs differ by subject domain. 'aho tuaiwi' is listed under Putaiao and again under Hauora; '(katu) noho haukori' under Tikanga a-Iwi and under Hauora. paekupu is a curriculum glossary and the same term legitimately appears in several subject lists. Recorded as a NEGATIVE result so the sweep stops re-deriving it: these are not duplicates to remove but one concept with several domains, and collapsing them is the concept layer's job. The same structure is what makes D29 safe.
findings.subject: paekupu entries sharing a headword and a gloss
findings.summary: 976 keys hold byte-identical glosses, and this is the source's structure, not a double import

findings.detail: hepatakakupu, kimikupu_hou, paekupu and te_aka write 'himoemoe' lower case with both macrons; te_matatiki and williams write 'Himoemoe', capitalised, with the same macrons. Recorded as the positive control for D18: Williams is macronised here, consistent with D18's finding that 31% of Williams headwords carry a macron, and the residual difference across the cluster is display capitalisation rather than orthography. Williams capitalising its main headwords is already documented as known-correct. Nothing to fix; this is what agreement looks like, and the concept layer should find no conflict here.
findings.subject: the himoemoe cluster
findings.summary: all six sources agree on himoemoe; only capitalisation differs

findings.detail: 24,900 of He Pataka Kupu's 24,941 senses carry a Maori gloss and none carries an English one. It is a monolingual Maori dictionary, so the absent gloss_en is the source's nature. Recorded because the shape looks exactly like the gap the normalisation brief asks to fill, and filling it would mean importing another dictionary's English into this one's entry - a breach of two hard rules at once. The English belongs on the concept record, which can hold both languages without either source losing its own voice.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:24133 has no English gloss
findings.summary: checked and it is by design, not a gap

findings.detail: rel_type 'citation' holds 213 rows corpus-wide whose target_headword is a reference like 'Tr. xliii, 466' - volume and page in the Transactions of the New Zealand Institute. These are not relations to any entry and never will be; they sit permanently in the unresolved count alongside relations that genuinely need judgement. Same shape as the D30 case just fixed and probably the same remedy - a citation belongs in a citation field, not in a target_headword. 213 rows is small, and unlike D30 nothing here is misread, so it is recorded rather than escalated.
findings.subject: williams:1252 relation citation -> 'Tr. xliii, 466'
findings.summary: a bibliographic citation is stored as a relation with an unresolvable target

findings.detail: ridge of a hill; line of descent (figurative, same word); to jerk a fishing line; weather-beaten or old; a dead branch; a pole fixed in a tree for a bird snare; old fish that have spawned; and inanga/whitebait, Galaxias maculatus. Plus two loans that correctly carry no etymology - te_aka:23941 'Hiwi' = Heaphy and te_aka:23942 'Hiwi' = Hivite. Williams gives three headwords (1250 jerk, 1251 ridge + descent, 1252 the four-sense cluster) and He Pataka Kupu gives seven separate entry rows. This is the strongest argument in the slice so far that the concept layer must key on sense rather than headword: keyed on the headword, hiwi would become one concept with eight incompatible meanings and three etymologies.
findings.subject: the hiwi cluster as a whole
findings.summary: eighteen entries on this key are eight unrelated words plus two loans

findings.detail: Tregear HOATU 'to give, away from the person speaking' is attached to all of them and belongs on all of them: unlike hia and hiwi, hoatu is one word throughout - give away from the speaker, and by extension put, hand over, and go on ahead. Recorded as a POSITIVE CONTROL so the standard is visible in both directions; a sweep that only ever reports splits is not being calibrated. Two residual issues, neither a mis-assignment: te_aka:1307 and williams:1267 carry the link at entry level with no sense, and both have multiple senses, so the addressability work still applies. And there is no POLLEX set at all, which is correct and informative - see the next finding.
findings.subject: all 20 hoatu entries
findings.summary: one cognate source on every entry, and for once that is right

findings.detail: The relation reads note 'no entry under this word in He Pataka Kupu' and target_entry_id NULL - the source names aho poka as a synonym for the garment cords and does not define it. Before D30 this was '(aho poka )' with the parens in the term, sitting in the unresolved queue as a judgement waiting to be made. It now reads as a term and is labelled as having no target. Recorded as a positive control on a fix from two clusters ago, verified in the data rather than in a test.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:4411#4 synonym -> 'aho poka'

findings.detail: ear lobe; gusset or fullness in a cloak; far off; deaf; obstinate; earwax; noisy, uproarious; the conjunction 'well, and so' (a shortened form of heoi, which williams:1298 and te_aka:1332 both state); 'that's enough' (papakupu:453, the same particle used differently); and paekupu's hoi 'soy, soya', correctly marked 'He kupu mino.' and correctly carrying no etymology. findings.detail: 'Homaitia e koutou ngā kōrero tootika...', 'I homaitia tērā mea...', 'E hoomaitia ana ērā mea.', 'I hoomaia ngā purapura ki ahau e Hera.' The entry is glossed 'give, bring to speaker, receive' with part of speech Universal, and the passive forms homaitia / hoomaitia / hoomaia are only visible in the examples. Te Aka states the same fact explicitly in its gloss - '(-hia,-ngia,-tia) ... does not take a passive ending when used as a command and traditionally never took one'. Not a defect: papakupu's examples are doing the work its gloss does not. Recorded because a concept record drawing only on glosses would lose the passive paradigm that the examples attest.
findings.subject: papakupu:476 examples

findings.detail: D30: hepatakakupu:13308's synonym reads 'hua paru' with note 'no entry under this word in He Pataka Kupu', and that is exactly true - no source headwords it. The marker is accurate, not merely applied. D32: williams:1540's see_also carries note 'hua (i)' and resolves to williams:1494, whose roman marker is i; the three other hua entries are handspike, the verb 'name' and 'buttocks'. Before D32 this would have been decided by list position. D34: hepatakakupu's identical-definition convention is what shows huatea and huamutu to be one synonym set. Recorded as a deliberate audit of prior fixes rather than as a new finding - the calibration is worth as much for confirming what now works as for finding what does not.
findings.subject: D30, D32 and D34 verified in the data
findings.summary: three fixes from earlier clusters are behaving correctly here, on cases they were not written against

findings.detail: Williams prints 'Taku he ki te huatea; no muri au i kite ai i te huauri' from its proverb collection. te_aka:15728#2 carries it inside a longer passage about Tamanuhiri and Hinenui, cited to Te Puke ki Hikurangi 31/7/1900:4 - a newspaper, not Williams. So unlike the Te Aka quotations found at himoemoe and hiwi, this is genuine independent attestation of the same proverb rather than one dictionary quoting another. Recorded because the concept layer needs to tell those two cases apart, and the citation is what distinguishes them.

findings.detail: The Maori reflex for TA.huri- is 'Huri/pari'. Before D33 the '/' was read as a separator, so this set keyed to `huri` and to `pari` - attaching 'Element in words for hurricane, cyclone' to every entry meaning 'turn, overturn' and every entry meaning 'cliff', while huripari itself got nothing. It now reaches 0 huri entries, 0 pari entries and 9 huripari entries. The sister languages make the convention unmistakable: Mangaia 'Uri/'ia, Manihiki 'Huri/hia', Tahitian 'Huri/fenua', Tuamotu 'Huri/popoo' - every one a compound of the same element. Recorded as a POSITIVE CONTROL on a fix from three clusters ago, verified in data it was not written against.
findings.subject: TA.huri- -> all 9 huripari entries
findings.summary: one cognate set, correctly on every entry, and it is the D33 fix demonstrating itself

findings.detail: 'Element in words for ?hurricane, cyclone?' should carry quotation marks; 'Cat?s cradle, string games', 'Turn one?s back on', 'that?s it!' should carry apostrophes - all are U+0294 LATIN LETTER GLOTTAL STOP. But NP.AATI 'Join together as a group (of people): (?)aati' uses the same character as a genuine Polynesian glottal, which is what makes this unfixable by rule. 18 of 3,291 cognateset descriptions and 0 of 49,760 reflex glosses, so it is confined and small. Recorded rather than escalated: distinguishing a mangled quote from a real glottal is judgement, and at 18 rows the judgement is cheaper than the rule.
findings.subject: U+0294 in 18 POLLEX cognate-set descriptions
findings.summary: an apostrophe rendered as a glottal stop, and not always distinguishable from a real one

findings.detail: Both headwords are 'ainga whakararo' with identical macronisation. paekupu glosses it 'subduction' under domain Putaiao/Science and records its components as 'ainga - driving force' and 'whakararo - downward'; te_aka glosses 'forcing downwards, subduction - a geological process where one tectonic plate moves under another' and cites Te Reo Putaiao 2009:305. te_aka's gloss spells out exactly the formation paekupu's component notes describe, and nothing in either contradicts the other. The difference is depth of definition, which section 3 treats as editorial rather than error. Concept 2599223 already proposes both; this confirms the two memberships rather than proposing a grouping.

They differ only in domain, Hangarau/Technology against Matauranga Whanui/Education General. paekupu publishes per curriculum subject, so listing a coined term under two areas is its structure rather than a data defect - but they are one word, and concepts 2599598 and 2599599 hold them separately. Systemic: 2,117 paekupu headwords appear on more than one entry, 833 of those with an identical gloss, and ALL 2,117 land in more than one concept. The concept builder seeds on lexeme, so two slugs from one source are two seeds and nothing rejoins them. Memberships deliberately NOT confirmed here: confirming both would assert the split is right, which is the opposite of this finding.
