findings.summary: the mythological stone-name set matches no sense any source records

findings.detail: Te Aka and Williams both hold it as a single seven-sense entry. He Pataka Kupu splits the senses across six entries that share a headword. Ngata reaches it from five English lemmas — Reception, Wedding breakfast, Celebrate, Celebration, Feast. Taikupu records only the roe sense. The concept is one word; the row counts are artefacts of how each dictionary is organised, which is exactly why provenance is kept rather than merged.
findings.subject: ngata (5 entries) ; hepatakakupu (6 entries) ; te_aka:755 ; williams:666 ; taikupu
findings.summary: one polysemous word, split three different ways by three different lookup directions

findings.detail: hepatakakupu:24516#6 glosses 'Ka whakapai i te ahua o nga makawe' — to improve the appearance of the hair — and Williams and Te Aka carry the same sense. Coconut flesh, molluscs, a gift and a mythological stone are all unrelated to it. Williams's own examples for the sense ('Kia hakaritia te mahunga', 'ki te hakari i tana tamahine') confirm the grooming reading, so this is an unattached sense rather than a doubtful one.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:24516#6 ; te_aka:755#1 ; williams:666#7
findings.summary: 'adorn, dress the hair' carries all four sets and is descended from none of them

findings.detail: 21 links, 7 entries, 3 sets. The cluster holds exactly two Maori senses and they divide cleanly. Anatomy: hepatakakupu:6895#1 'Te tua o te upoko mai i te papahuaki ki te honotanga ki te kaki' and tregear_exceptions:WR-TE.70 'The back of the skull.' — those two, and only those two, belong to HAMU 'the back of the skull'. Gleaning: te_aka:804 (both senses), williams:734#1, papakupu:304#1, hepatakakupu:14503#1 'Ka kohi haere i nga maramara, i nga para', te_matatiki 'Scavenger' — those belong to HAMU 'to gather sparsely scattered things' and to PN.SAMU.1A 'Eat scraps', which is the actual Proto-Polynesian ancestor. About twelve of the twenty-one links are right.
findings.subject: all 7 non-loan hamu entries <- HAMU 'back of the skull' / HAMU 'gather sparsely scattered things' / PN.SAMU.1A 'Eat scraps'
findings.summary: two mutually exclusive senses, three cognate sets, and every set attached to every entry

findings.detail: Both gloss 'shirt.' and both are haate. 22815 carries loan_marker 'Historical Loan Word' with a long example about wrapping a newborn's navel; 916 is [loan, noun] with no example. Within-source duplicate: 916 looks like the shorter modern entry and 22815 the historical citation. Queued rather than applied — naming a canonical row is a judgement, and merging rows is not a field patch.
findings.subject: te_aka:22815 ; te_aka:916
findings.summary: Te Aka holds 'shirt' twice, marked as a loan two different ways

findings.detail: It also pollutes the matcher: 'ene' becomes a content word of the gloss, so it counts toward coverage and distinctiveness against every other source's gloss. Williams's '=' convention may already be handled elsewhere in the xref work; recorded here as evidence rather than assumed new.
findings.subject: williams:1056
findings.summary: gloss_en is 'Anus. = ene.' — the '= ene' is a cross-reference to another headword carried inside the gloss text rather than as a relation.

findings.detail: The source reads 'Hereputia tonutia atu e au; te ! ka mau.' — one example in two clauses. The extraction ends the Maori run at the '!' and the clause after it begins lower case, so it never starts a new run and stays in the gloss. He Pataka Kupu carries the same sentence whole: 'Herepūtia tonutia atu e au, tē! Ka mau. (W 46)'. NOT ESCALATED as a pipeline fix: 293 glosses end in a lower-case Maori clause after a terminator, but only about half are this shape — 'ao (i).' and 'apa (iii).' are cross-references and 'apaapa wahie.' is a compound, not a stranded sentence. Separating them needs the judgement this sweep exists for, so it stays per-cluster work.
findings.subject: williams:1073#2
findings.summary: the tail of the example is stranded in the gloss: 'Seize, catch and hold firmly. ka mau.'

findings.detail: Both give herepū, and they correspond exactly to te_aka:1095#2 and #1. Neither ngata entry for 'Tie' carries an example, because the sentence there uses ponaia rather than herepū — the D15 example-owner fix placing it on the entry it actually illustrates.
findings.subject: ngata:WR-HMN.11412#42229~1 ; ngata:WR-HMN.13122#45243~3
findings.summary: 'Seize' and 'Tie' are the same word reached from two English lemmas

findings.detail: HEREPU glosses 'to seize, to catch and hold firmly. Cf. herehere, to tie'. Its own cross-reference to herehere is the point: the 'tie up in bundles' sense (te_aka:1095#1, williams:1073#1, hepatakakupu:30113#1) and the 'seize' sense (te_aka:1095#2, williams:1073#2, hepatakakupu:26870#2) both descend from here rather than competing. te_aka:1095#3 'embargo.' is a modern coinage extending the seize sense. An anchoring judgement, not an exclusion — the whole cluster is one etymology.
findings.subject: te_aka:1095 ; williams:1073
findings.summary: two multi-sense entries carry the Tregear HEREPU link with no sense assigned, and it fits both senses of each

findings.detail: te_matatiki glosses '(seize goods etc.) embargo' and derives it from W.46 'seize, catch and hold firmly', resolving to williams:1073. te_aka:1095#3 is simply 'embargo.' Third instance in this calibration of Te Aka absorbing a Te Matatiki coinage, after 'atea' (cricket off-side) and the same pattern in 'angitu'. The concept layer will need to represent that one dictionary in this corpus quotes another, or the corpus will read as independent attestation where it has one source.
findings.subject: te_aka:1095#3 ; te_matatiki:WR-TM.411#48037
findings.summary: the coined 'embargo' sense is in both Te Aka and Te Matatiki

findings.detail: This is the sense-anchoring problem in its purest form: 7 sets x 9 entries, matched on spelling alone, where the correct assignment is one-to-few. AN.FIHA.A 'How many? how much?' and Tregear HIA '“How many?” When used in speaking of persons, toko is prefixed' belong to the interrogative numeral - hepatakakupu:30371#1, papakupu:395#1, te_aka:1129#1, te_aka:1129#2, williams:1090#1. PN.FIHA.B 'Few, a few' belongs to the indefinite quantifier - hepatakakupu:30372#2, te_aka:1129#3, williams:1090#2. CP.FIA- 'Verbal prefix indicating desire, wish' and Tregear HIA 'HIAHIA, a desire, wish' belong to the desiderative prefix - papakupu:396#1 (whose own gloss lists hiamoe, hiainu, hiakai) and williams:1091#1-2 'Desire, wish / Be in love with'. Tregear HIA 'with difficulty; hardly to be performed' belongs to williams:1092#1 'used to express surprise and admiration', whose first example glosses as 'what difficulty you must have had in coming through on the high tide'. TA.FIA.* 'Where?' is Tahitic and has no reflex in this cluster; it should attach to none of them. Williams separates these as three numbered headwords (1090, 1091, 1092), so the corpus already contains the evidence for the split - it is simply not being read by a headword_exact match.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:30371#1 ; hepatakakupu:30372#2 ; papakupu:395#1 ; papakupu:396#1 ; te_aka:1129#1-3 ; williams:1090#1-2 ; williams:1091#1-2 ; williams:1092#1
findings.summary: seven cognate sets are attached to every hia entry, but they belong to four different words

findings.detail: The ngata entry glosses 'Draw', with the example 'Hia te nga hohonu' / 'Draw a deep breath', and its own definition_raw reads 'hii, hiia Draw a deep breath' - it is the passive of hii 'raise, haul up', and ngata itself files it as a synonym of hii. It shares a search key with hia 'how many' only because normalise_search_key strips the macron. Every one of the seven sets is wrong on it, including the two that are right elsewhere in this cluster. Not a D23-class fix: nothing marks this entry as a loan or as anything else mechanically separable - the macron is the whole of the evidence, and acting on it is exactly the concept-layer judgement D18 is waiting for. A concrete argument for macron-sensitivity as a tie-breaker once concepts exist.
findings.subject: ngata:WR-HMN.3206#30324~2#1
findings.summary: hiaa is not hia at all - it is hii + -a, and it carries all seven cognate sets

findings.detail: 'hiamoe sleepy, hiatangi on the verge of tears, hiangongo pine away, hiainu thirsty, hiakai hungry' - five headwords with their glosses, packed into the definition of the prefix that forms them. Each exists as its own papakupu entry. Queued rather than patched: emitting five derived_form or see_also relations is a structural change, not a field correction, and the rubric keeps relation-creation out of the patch layer.
findings.subject: papakupu:396#1
findings.summary: the gloss is a run-on list of five compounds that should be cross-references

findings.detail: e, kia, toko-, tua- and whia are the particles sense 1's gloss says hia 'combines with' - grammatical context, not synonymy. tini, tokomaha, maha, marea, nui, takitini and tuauriuri are genuine synonyms, but of sense 3 'several, a number of, many', not of the interrogative. All twenty hang off the entry with no sense attached, so the app cannot tell the two groups apart. Same shape as the etymology finding above and fixed by the same thing - sense-level attachment - which is why it is recorded rather than patched. Note the list is not derived from the gloss: the gloss names ka, which is absent from the relations.
findings.subject: te_aka:1129 relations
findings.summary: twenty synonym relations mix sense 1's combining particles with sense 3's actual synonyms

findings.detail: Not patched: gloss_en alone could be trimmed to 'Head of a river.' but the entry also carries another word's example, citation and second sense, so a one-field patch would leave it half wrong and looking right. The entry id 1114701 is itself anomalous — every other williams id in these clusters is three or four digits (898, 1056, 1114) — which suggests the boundary miss also produced a synthesised id and may be findable by that shape. Consequence beyond this entry: the foreign text inflates the gloss's content words, so coverage against te_aka's 'head (of a river), headwater.' is diluted and the correct three-source merge does not form.
findings.subject: williams:1114701
findings.summary: The entry has swallowed the following headword. gloss_en reads 'Head of a river. whakahiku, 1. n. Present brought in large quantities.' — only the first sentence is hikunga's. The example ('...he whakahiku ki tana kai...') and the whole of sense 2 ('? To follow on, commence.', example 'ka whakahikuhiku te takurua') belong to whakahiku / whakahikuhiku.

findings.detail: himoemoe has no etymology at all, in any of its six entries. Te Matatiki states the derivation in its own prose - 'himoemoe W.50 acid, sour / moemoe W.205 sour, acid, i.e., causing one to close the eyes' - and both cross-references resolve correctly to williams:1163 and williams:1503304, so the corpus holds the chain. But moemoe carries 0 cognate sets while moe carries 5, and nothing connects them. Measured across the corpus: 257 full reduplications (1,158 entries) and 863 whaka- causatives (2,853 entries) carry no etymology while their base does - about 4,011 entries. This is NOT a pipeline fix and must not become one: attaching moe's Proto-Polynesian sets to moemoe would assert POLLEX claims something it does not, which is inventing lexicographic content. The right shape is a derivation relation - entry to base entry, naming the process - kept out of ETY_* for the same reason loan_origin is, so the app can walk himoemoe -> moemoe -> moe -> PPN without any layer claiming a cognate it was not given.
findings.subject: the himoemoe cluster ; moemoe ; moe
findings.summary: the etymology layer is morphologically blind, and about 4,000 entries lose their ancestry to it

findings.detail: te_aka:11754's example is verbatim hepatakakupu:24133's - 'Te himoemoe hoki o te aporo nei - kaore e kore i whakia matatia mai.' - and te_aka cites it honestly as 'He Pataka Kupu: Te Kai a te Rangatira 2008:112'. te_matatiki derives its entry from Williams W.50 and its cross-references resolve to williams:1163. So of six sources, the independent attestations are Williams, He Pataka Kupu, and the coinage tradition that paekupu and kimikupu_hou share. Corpus-wide this is measurable and attributed: 2,845 of te_aka's 23,537 cited examples (12%) name another source in this corpus - 1,755 Williams, 1,099 He Pataka Kupu. A concept record must count attestations, not rows, or an eleven-source corpus will read as eleven independent witnesses where it has three.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:24133 ; te_aka:11754 ; te_matatiki:WR-TM.454#48080 ; williams:1163 ; kimikupu_hou:WR-KKH.182#52905~1 ; paekupu:himoemoe
findings.summary: six witnesses to one concept, but at least three of them are quoting the other three

findings.detail: paekupu:aeha cross_ref -> 'aeha' note 'aeha - interjection denoting annoyance'; paekupu:ahua-maoa cross_ref -> 'maoa' note 'maoa - be cooked'. These are the component annotations LOAN_ORIGIN_DESIGN section 4 identifies as the corpus's richest loan-origin rows - Maori form, gloss, and sometimes a loan flag together. For a single-component term the component is the headword, so the relation points home and carries no information as a relation, while the note carries the real data. 170 in paekupu, 6 papakupu, 1 temarareo, plus 8 already resolved to their own entry. Queued rather than fixed: deleting the relation would destroy the component gloss, and relocating it needs the component model that is designed but not built. NOT included in that count: te_matatiki's 204 similar-looking rows, which are unresolved cross-source citations of Williams and a different problem.
findings.subject: paekupu self-referential cross_ref relations
findings.summary: about 185 relations point an entry at itself, carrying a component gloss in the note

findings.detail: CE.SIWI.* 'Ridge of hill' and Tregear HIWI 'the ridge of a hill' belong to the ridge word - williams:1251#1, te_aka:1284#1, papakupu:442#1, hepatakakupu:19969#1 and hepatakakupu:20526#2 - and arguably to williams:1251#2 'Line of descent', which is the same word used figuratively and is matched by hepatakakupu:15554#3 'te taura e here ana i te tangata ki ona tupuna'. Tregear HIWI 'to jerk a fishing-line' belongs to the jerk word - williams:1250#1, te_aka:1283#1, hepatakakupu:26659#1 - and its Tregear citation is the same sentence Williams quotes, 'Katahi ano ka hiwia e ia'. The remaining words have NO etymology in the corpus and should carry none: weather-beaten (williams:1252#1, te_aka:41235#1, ngata:WR-HMN.14313#47040~1#1), dead branch (williams:1252#2, te_aka:41235#2, hepatakakupu:2263#3), the bird-snare pole (williams:1252#3, hepatakakupu:10279#5), the spawned-out fish (williams:1252#4) and the whitebait (te_aka:43534#1, hepatakakupu:13897#4). Williams splits the cluster into exactly three numbered headwords and every other source's senses land inside that partition, so the evidence for the split is already in the corpus.
findings.subject: all 15 non-loan hiwi entries
findings.summary: three etymology sources are attached to every entry, and only two of the eight words have any ancestry at all

findings.detail: hepatakakupu:19969#1, 20526#2, 15554#3, 13897#4 and 10279#5 form a clean 1-2-3-4-5 run under this headword, while 26659#1 and 2263#3 belong to a different run. The builder's own comment records why - He Pataka Kupu's word_id repeats across senses so the row PK is used as source_entry_id, with word_id kept in locator 'for provenance / sense grouping'. So the grouping IS recoverable, via entry.locator, and the batch assembler does not currently surface it. Recorded because it materially helps the concept layer: for this source the source itself already says which senses belong to one lemma, and reading it is cheaper than inferring it. Not escalated - nothing is wrong with the data, only with what the sweep can see of it.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu sense numbering across separate entry rows
findings.summary: one dictionary entry is scattered over five rows and only sense_number reconstructs it

findings.detail: te_aka:41235#1 'to become weather-beaten, weather' carries the example 'Whakairia te mutu kia hiwia' cited 'W 1971:54' - the same sentence williams:1252#1 prints. te_aka:41235#2 'dead branch' is williams:1252#2, and hepatakakupu:2263#3 'he manga rakau kua maroke, kua mate' is the same sense again in Maori. ngata's 'Weatherbeaten' is a fourth witness to the first. Te Aka takes two of Williams's four senses and leaves the bird-snare pole and the spawned-out fish behind, which is the shape a concept record has to represent: partial uptake, not a clean one-to-one merge.
findings.subject: williams:1252 ; te_aka:41235 ; ngata:WR-HMN.14313#47040~1 ; hepatakakupu:2263#3
findings.summary: Te Aka's entry is Williams's first two senses, quoted with attribution

findings.detail: te_aka:43534#1 gives a full species treatment - 'inanga, whitebait, Galaxias maculatus - a small silvery-white native fish... Maximum size 190 mm' - and hepatakakupu:13897#4 gives 'he ika wai maori e 8-10 henemita te tipu', a freshwater fish 8-10 cm long. Same referent, and distinct from williams:1252#4 'old fish that have spawned and are in poor condition', which is a condition rather than a species. Worth separating carefully in the concept layer, because the two fish senses would collapse on a naive gloss match.
findings.subject: te_aka:43534#1 ; hepatakakupu:13897#4
findings.summary: the whitebait sense is in two sources and in neither of the dictionaries that define the other seven

findings.detail: williams:1256 reads 'Ho. A verb used only in the compound forms, hoake, hoatu, homai, q.v' - Williams naming the bound base and the three compounds it forms. hoatu is ho + atu, the directional 'away from speaker', which is exactly why its gloss is 'give, AWAY FROM THE SPEAKER' and why homai is the reciprocal. hoatu itself carries no POLLEX set, correctly, because it is a Maori-internal compound rather than a reconstructed protoform - but ho carries 6 cognate sets and atu carries 6, so the ancestry is present and unreachable. This is the WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN case with the evidence already resolved to an entry rather than needing to be parsed: a derivation relation would join hoatu -> ho -> PPN without any layer claiming a cognate it was not given.
findings.subject: williams:1267 see_also -> williams:1256 'Ho'
findings.summary: the corpus states this word's formation outright and the etymology layer cannot see it

findings.detail: The three targets are fragments of this entry's own gloss, 'give (away from speaker), go ahead'. Worse elsewhere: papakupu:87 anana carries see_also ['Yikes!','The','hens','have','been','messing','things','up!'] - an English example sentence split on whitespace - and four entries carry 'the entry for Maramataka] [151204]', where the real target Maramataka is buried in the connective words and the closing bracket. 120 of papakupu's 1,163 see_also values contain letters outside the Maori alphabet and so cannot be headwords. MEASURED AND NOT ESCALATED: the fault is in 02_papakupu_extract, which reads the source PDF, and the recovery is a heuristic - find the Maori headword inside English prose - that would resolve about 58 and invent the rest. That is the class of rule D31 was deliberately kept narrow to avoid. Note the bulk of papakupu's 744 unresolved see_also are NOT this: 'whakaaetia', 'akina', 'mautohe' are real Maori words that simply have no papakupu entry.
findings.subject: papakupu:447 see_also -> 'Hoatu!' ; 'Go' ; 'ahead!'
findings.summary: English prose is being shredded into one cross-reference per word

findings.detail: Donate, Feed, Give, Give in, Hand over, Let, Offer, Part with, Pass, Put forth, Put forward, Tip, Turn over. Ngata is an English-to-Maori dictionary, so this is its correct structure, not duplication to remove - but for the concept layer it means one concept has fourteen ngata witnesses that are really one witness seen from thirteen angles. Counting rows here would weight ngata thirteen times against Williams's one entry. Same lesson as the Te Aka quotation finding at himoemoe, from the opposite direction: the corpus's row counts are not attestation counts.
findings.subject: 14 ngata entries with headword hoatu
findings.summary: one Maori word reached from thirteen English lemmas

findings.detail: waiho, neke atu, whiu, whoatu, whiuwhiu, maka, makamaka, uaki, pei, utu. utu belongs to sense 1's 'pay'; neke atu and waiho to sense 2's 'you go ahead, go on'; maka, whiu and whiuwhiu are the throwing sense of 'put'. None carries a sense. Same shape as te_aka:1129 at hia and fixed by the same sense-level attachment, recorded here because the two senses are further apart than usual - 'give someone something' and 'you go on ahead' - so an app showing all ten under either one is visibly wrong rather than merely imprecise.
findings.subject: te_aka:1307 relations
findings.summary: ten synonyms hang off the entry undifferentiated across two quite different senses

findings.detail: Give (20566#1), move something to an appointed place (20898#2), and the command to go on ahead (14776#3) - the same three senses Williams and Te Aka carry, in the same order, scattered across three rows whose only link is sense_number and the shared word_id in entry.locator. Second sighting after hiwi, which makes it the source's regular structure rather than an accident, and confirms that entry.locator already reconstructs the lemma for this source. Worth surfacing in the batch assembler before the supervisor runs, since it is free grouping evidence the sweep currently cannot see.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:20566#1 ; 20898#2 ; 14776#3
findings.summary: a clean 1-2-3 sense run split across three entry rows, again

findings.detail: After D33 the cluster carries only Tregear HOI 'the lobe of the ear. 2. The gusset of a garment. Cf. tihoi'. Those two senses are exactly williams:1295#1 'Lobe of the ear' and #2 'Fullness in a cloak to make it fit over the shoulders', and exactly te_aka:1331#4 'ear lobe' and #5 'fullness - of a cloak', in the same order - three sources agreeing sense-for-sense. It also covers hepatakakupu:8621#2 (the soft part of the lower ear) and hepatakakupu:4411#4 (the cords set into a garment). It does NOT cover hoi 'far off' (williams:1296, te_aka:1331#1, hepatakakupu:2833#2), hoi 'deaf, obstinate' (williams:1297#2, te_aka:1331#2-3, hepatakakupu:226#1, 18537#4, taikupu 'disobedient'), hoi 'earwax' (williams:1297#1, hepatakakupu:27116#5), hoi 'noisy' (williams:1297#3, hepatakakupu:25746#3) or the particle hoi (williams:1298, te_aka:1332, papakupu:453, hepatakakupu:26311#3). Williams's four numbered headwords partition the cluster and the corpus already holds the evidence.
findings.subject: williams:1295#1-2 ; te_aka:1331#4-5 ; the remaining hoi entries
findings.summary: one Tregear set remains and it fits two senses precisely, not the other eight

findings.detail: ngata's 'Ear lobe' record lists hoi, pokopoko, toke and both its synonym relations resolve. hepatakakupu:8621#2 names the same pair and neither resolves, because more than one He Pataka Kupu entry carries those headwords and the resolver will not guess. Not a defect - it is D19's documented boundary, and D29 could not help because the candidates share a domain. Recorded because the answer is sitting in the adjacent source: two dictionaries agree on the synonym set, and the concept layer can carry the resolution that neither source alone licenses.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:8621#2 ; ngata:WR-HMN.3333#30537
findings.summary: the same three ear-lobe synonyms, resolved in one source and unresolved in the other

findings.detail: whakaturi, taringa pakura, kaki maro, tohetohe, turi, ngana, makiki, koioio, whakatete, whakatohe, whatuturi, koroiroi, pukutohe, pukeke, houkeke, upoko maro, papamaro, hokeke, whakatuturi, motohe, pake, taumaro, pukutohetohe. All are 'deaf' or 'obstinate' - senses 2 and 3 - and none belongs to 'far off', 'ear lobe' or 'fullness in a cloak'. The most lopsided case in the slice so far: 23 relations, 0 of them attached to a sense, on an entry where 3 of the 5 senses should carry none. Fixed by sense-level attachment, the same remedy as hia and hoatu.
findings.subject: te_aka:1331 relations
findings.summary: twenty-three synonyms hang off a five-sense entry, and every one of them belongs to two of those senses

findings.detail: word_id 988 is 'homai' with senses 1-3; word_id 1341 is 'hōmai' with senses 1-2. The matching senses carry byte-identical definitions: 'Ka whakahau kia whāia tētahi huarahi...' appears under both, as does 'Ka tuku noa, ka whakawhiti noa i tētahi mea...' and 'Ka hari mai...'. Checked the landing table before concluding anything: both lemmas are in the source, so this is the source's duplicate and not the pipeline's. 988 is the fuller entry - it carries a third sense, the whakaropiropi hand game, which 1341 lacks and which te_aka:1371#3 also records, citing He Pātaka Kupu 2008:126. The concept layer should treat 988 and 1341 as one word with three senses and prefer the macronised spelling, which every other source in this cluster except Williams and Te Aka uses.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu word_id=988 'homai' ; word_id=1341 'hōmai'
findings.summary: He Pātaka Kupu holds this word twice, once unmacronised and once macronised, with identical definitions

findings.detail: Put forth, Render, Turn over, Give (three separate records), Hold out. ngata:WR-HMN.13572#46068 is the same record judged at hoatu: its ~1 and ~2 are hōmai and hōmaitia, its ~3 and ~4 are hoatu and hoatutia, all four glossed 'Turn over'. So a single Ngata record contributes entries to two different clusters, and the example 'Kua hōmaitia e to mātau matua te pāmu ki ahau' correctly attaches only to the hōmai side under D15. Recorded because the concept layer will meet the same record twice and must not double-count it.
findings.subject: 9 ngata entries with headword hōmai
findings.summary: one word reached from seven English lemmas, and one record shared with hoatu

findings.detail: williams:1256 'Ho. A verb used only in the compound forms, hoake, hoatu, homai, q.v' names all three compounds outright. homai is hō + mai (toward the speaker) and hoatu is hō + atu (away from the speaker), which is exactly what their glosses say - te_aka:1371 'to give (towards the speaker)' against te_aka:1307 'to give (away from the speaker)'. Neither compound carries a POLLEX set, correctly; the base does. Second sighting of this pattern after hoatu two clusters ago, and stronger here because the two compounds are in the same cluster group and differ only in the directional. WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN's step 1 would capture both from evidence already resolved to an entry.
findings.subject: homai ; hoatu ; the bound base hō
findings.summary: the pair homai and hoatu is the clearest derivation evidence the corpus holds

findings.detail: Macronised: papakupu:476 'hōmai', tregear_exceptions 'Hōmai', all seven ngata entries 'hōmai'. Unmacronised: williams:1335 'Homai', te_aka:1371 'homai'. He Pātaka Kupu carries both. papakupu also records a variant form 'hoomai' and its examples show 'homaitia', 'hoomaitia' and 'hoomaia' side by side, which is the double-vowel convention rather than a third spelling. The modern consensus is hōmai - the vowel is long because the word is hō + mai, the same hō that williams:1256 defines as 'a verb used only in the compound forms, hoake, hoatu, homai' - so this is a case where the word-formation evidence decides the orthography. Recorded for D18 as a worked example where the macron is derivable from morphology rather than from a vote among sources.
findings.subject: the homai cluster across six sources
findings.summary: sources split on the macron and one source takes both sides

findings.detail: huatea carries no cognate set in any of its nine entries. It is hua + tea - 'roe, egg, fruit' plus 'white, pale' - which is exactly why it means milt, the white reproductive fluid of a male fish. williams:1540 states it: see_also -> williams:1494 with note 'hua (i)', and 1494 is the Fruit/Egg/Roe entry, not the handspike (ii), the verb 'name' (iii) or 'buttocks' (iv). hua carries 8 cognate sets and tea carries 3, so the ancestry is present and unreachable. Third sighting in three clusters after hoatu and homai, and the strongest yet because the source resolved the homograph for us. WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN step 1 captures this from a reference that already points at an entry.
findings.subject: the huatea cluster ; williams:1494 'Hua' ; tea
findings.summary: no etymology at all, and the corpus states the derivation with the homograph already picked out

findings.detail: williams:1540#1 reads 'Milt of a fish, roe of an eel.' te_aka:41381 gives #1 'milt, sperm-filled reproductive gland of a male fish' and #2 'eel roe'. He Pataka Kupu gives the same two as separate entries, 13308#1 and 13307#2. Three sources, one concept, and the finer-grained split is the better record - this is a case where merging to the coarsest source would lose information the corpus has. Worth keeping as a worked example of why a concept record needs to hold a sense inventory rather than a single gloss.
findings.subject: williams:1540#1 ; te_aka:41381#1-2 ; hepatakakupu:13308#1 ; hepatakakupu:13307#2
findings.summary: one Williams sense is split into exactly two senses by two other sources, in the same order

findings.detail: huamutu is not a paekupu headword, so the relation dangles. But hepatakakupu:15227 glosses huamutu 'Kaore i whai uri' - byte-identical to hepatakakupu:15224#2's gloss for huatea - so the two are in the same He Pataka Kupu synonym set and paekupu's assertion is right. williams:1512 carries the same pairing, glossing huamutu 'Having no descendants' alongside its whelk senses. This is the shape D34 fixes within a source and cannot fix across one: 4,841 of paekupu's 8,028 unresolved relations name a target paekupu does not define. Unlike He Pataka Kupu, paekupu has no marker saying so, which is why these look like failures rather than statements.
findings.subject: paekupu:huatea synonym -> 'huamutu'
findings.summary: the link is correct and unresolvable, and an adjacent source proves it

findings.detail: williams:1494#3 reads 'Roe of a fish. Hua rakau, spawn; hua paru, milt.' - two compounds with their glosses, packed into the parent sense. hua paru exists nowhere in the corpus as a headword, so the only place it is defined is inside another entry's running text. 353 williams senses carry this shape: 'Aho tahuhu, first weft in weaving a garment', 'Atawhai kino, unfriendly, malicious', 'Heke haere, decrease', 'Ata po, before dawn; ata puao, ata iti, early dawn'. NOT ESCALATED: the boundary between a sub-entry and ordinary prose is judgement - the same probe also catches 'Sometimes translated day before yesterday' - and extracting them creates entries the source did not headword. This is WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN's 'attested, needs parsing' bucket: each one is a derived form with its base and its gloss, which is precisely what derivation.base_form and base_gloss are for.
findings.subject: 353 williams senses carrying a compound sub-definition
findings.summary: Williams defines derived terms inside the parent's gloss, and hua paru is one of them

findings.detail: huatea 'milt of a fish, roe of an eel' - williams:1540, te_aka:41381, hepatakakupu:13308#1 (milt, 'te wai tatea o te ika') and 13307#2 (eel roe, 'nga hua i te kopu o te uwha tuna'). huatea 'childless' - williams:1541#1, te_aka:15728, hepatakakupu:15224#2, ngata and paekupu. Only williams:1541#2 carries 'Some part of the Haliotis (paua)', and Williams files it as a second sense of the childless entry rather than a third headword, which is almost certainly a filing decision rather than a claim that the two are one word. Flagged so the concept layer does not inherit that grouping uncritically.
findings.subject: the huatea cluster as a whole
findings.summary: nine entries are two words, and one source keeps a third sense that no one else has

findings.detail: The protoform is written 'huri-' with a trailing hyphen and glossed as an element in words, not as a word. huripari is huri- + pari, and POLLEX has reconstructed the COMPOUND rather than leaving it to be inferred from the base - the opposite of moemoe, which carries nothing while moe carries five sets. This is exactly the case WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN section 4 rests on: POLLEX decides case by case whether a derived form is separately reconstructible, so its silence elsewhere is a judgement and not a gap. Recorded as confirmation of that argument from the affirmative side, which the note did not have an example of.
findings.subject: TA.huri- 'Element in words for hurricane, cyclone'
findings.summary: POLLEX names this a bound word-forming element, which is the distinction the word-formation note turns on

findings.detail: ngata:WR-HMN.14447 is the English entry 'Wind', and it lists about fifteen separate Maori equivalents each as its own record with no body text: hauaauru, marangai, tonga, tonga maa uru, tonga waho, kootonga, puuhuka, haupongi, haupaauma, hauwhenua, koohengi, hauraro, paakihiroa, parera - and huripari. These are named winds. The projection gives every one of them gloss_en 'Wind', so huripari, a hurricane, reads as meaning 'wind'. The same word also appears under Tornado, Typhoon, Cyclone and Hurricane, where the lemma is a fair gloss. This is the deliberate D1-class decision that the English headword IS the gloss, and it is right for most of Ngata - but a concept layer merging glosses across sources must not treat 'Wind' as Ngata's definition of huripari alongside Te Aka's 'hurricane, cyclone, tornado, typhoon'. Only 390 of 33,775 ngata entries (1%) are bare lemma projections with neither body text nor example, so the exposure is small and identifiable.
findings.subject: ngata sense.gloss_en for all 33,775 entries
findings.summary: the gloss is the English lemma the word was listed under, not a definition of the word

findings.detail: Ngata lists huripari under Tornado, Typhoon, Cyclone, Hurricane and Wind. te_aka:1611#1 glosses it 'hurricane, cyclone, tornado, typhoon' - the same four, minus the loose one. williams:1680#1 has 'Fierce wind, hurricane', paekupu 'fierce wind, tornado', and hepatakakupu 'He aawhaa nui e tino kino ai te pupuhi o te hau'. Five sources, one concept, no disagreement anywhere - the rare case where dedup is unambiguous. Worth keeping as the shape a clean concept record takes, against which the contested ones can be compared.
findings.subject: 5 ngata entries ; te_aka:1611#1 ; williams:1680#1 ; paekupu:huripari ; hepatakakupu:26477#1
findings.summary: Te Aka's gloss is the union of Ngata's five English lemmas

findings.detail: hepatakakupu:300's synonym set is hikoki, hirori, huukeke, huurorirori, kaurori, kookeke, ruriruri, takarangi, turori, whakatiikorokoro, wherori - a set of words for staggering and reeling, of which hirori, turori, kaurori, wherori, huurorirori and hurori itself share -rori. rori carries 3 cognate sets, hirori 1 and turori 2, while hurori, wherori and kaurori carry none. The family is real and the coverage is arbitrary. Not actionable under the rubric - attaching rori's sets to hurori would assert a reconstruction POLLEX did not make - but it is another WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN case, and an unusually clear one because the source has already grouped the whole family as synonyms.
findings.subject: the -rori family
findings.summary: a transparent morphological family with patchy etymology and no link between its members

findings.detail: ngata:WR-HMN.12191 writes huurori; hepatakakupu, paekupu, te_aka and williams all write hurori. hepatakakupu's own synonym set for this word contains huurorirori and huukeke, both macronised, so the source is not simply macron-free. Recorded for D18 without a recommendation: unlike hoomai at the previous cluster, no morphological argument settles this one - hurori is not transparently huu + rori - so it needs the concept layer and a source-precedence rule rather than a derivation.
findings.subject: ngata 'huurori' against every other source's 'hurori'
findings.summary: one source macronises and five do not

findings.detail: 'Childhood, youth' - hepatakakupu:6269, papakupu:600, te_aka:15440#2, williams:1185301. 'The lesser part' - ngata under both Skerrick and Minority, te_aka:15440#1. Te Aka is the only source carrying both, and it orders them the other way round from everyone else. Not a defect; recorded because a concept layer merging on first-sense would pair Te Aka's 'minor, less important' with Williams's 'childhood' and produce a concept that is neither.
findings.subject: the itinga cluster
findings.summary: one word, two senses, and the sources split evenly between them

findings.detail: He Pataka Kupu says itinga's master definition is tamarikitanga, resolved to entry 6273 and sense 2337224. This is the case D35 exists for and it is more interesting than turori's: the master is a DIFFERENT WORD, not a spelling variant, so the source is asserting that itinga and tamarikitanga are one concept with one definition. That is a canonical-concept claim made by the lexicographers, addressed by id, and the concept layer can take it as given rather than inferring it from gloss overlap. Positive control recorded from data D35 was not written against.
findings.subject: hepatakakupu:6269 master_definition -> hepatakakupu:6273 'tamarikitanga'
findings.summary: D35 working in the very next cluster, and pointing across headwords

findings.detail: itinga is iti + -nga, the nominalisation, and its two senses are exactly what that predicts - 'childhood, the time of being small' and 'the lesser part, a minority'. iti carries 4 cognate sets and itinga carries 0. This is the -nga class WORD_FORMATION_DESIGN marks as unsafe to segment by rule, because runga is not ru + -nga and tonga is not to + -nga - so itinga is a case where the derivation is real and only judgement or an attested statement can establish it. D36 supplies the attested statement for Williams sub-entries generally, though not for this one, since Williams filed it under the wrong neighbour.
findings.subject: itinga ; iti
findings.summary: no etymology on itinga while iti carries four sets, and the -nga class is the one that cannot be automated

findings.detail: D35: He Pataka Kupu publishes a master_definition link on 14,379 senses; the parser never read it. D36: the Williams parser DID read parent_headword on 3,032 sub-entries and the import had no column for it. Both were structural statements by the source about which entry is canonical or basic, both addressed by id or by printed layout rather than by spelling, and both invisible from the unified tables the sweep reads. This suggests a targeted audit worth running once rather than waiting for clusters to stumble on it: for each source, compare the fields the parser emits against the columns the landing table holds, and the markup classes in the raw files against what the parser looks for. Recorded as a recommendation, not acted on.
findings.subject: the pattern behind D35 and D36
findings.summary: two consecutive clusters found the same class of loss - parsed, then dropped one step later

findings.detail: Corpus-wide: all 160,712 ETY_entry_link rows are match_method='headword_exact', and 133,943 of them (83%) belong to the 36,543 entries that carry MORE than one competing cognate set. Worst case is 'au' with 16 rival sets on one entry. This is the largest unresolved class in the corpus and it is judgement work, not a pipeline fix — deciding which set a sense descends from is exactly what the rubric's third question asks and what the sweep exists to answer. Recorded here with its scale so the scale is known before the long sweep begins.
findings.subject: KAHURANGI 'a variety of the volcanic stone called obsidian, of a reddish colour'
findings.summary: Attached to all 29 entries across all 7 sources, including te_aka:47064 'Blues - a rugby team from the northern North Island'. Nothing in this cluster means obsidian. The link is headword_exact — matched on the spelling KAHURANGI, never on meaning — and it fans out to every sense that shares the spelling.

findings.detail: Not diagnosed here. Coverage between te_aka:1885#1 'be blue, precious.' and paekupu 'blue, sky-blue' is roughly 0.33 on a shared 'blue' with a high df, so it grades weak — but weak is still evidence and should still attach, which points at a block rather than at the thresholds. Noted for a later look rather than guessed at.
findings.subject: concept 958830 / 958831
findings.summary: te_aka:1885 'be blue, precious.' sits in its own concept while ngata, paekupu, papakupu and te_matatiki share another one elected as 'blue, sky-blue'. Both describe the same word, and te_aka is the source that treats it as one entry with seven senses.

findings.detail: The correct assignment is visible from the sense inventory, which is the rubric's point about judging identity and etymology together rather than separately. Both Tregear sets currently attach to all of them, so the right answer and the wrong answer are recorded identically.
findings.subject: KAHURANGI 'unsettled, irresolute. Cf. karangi, restless; kahuirangi'
findings.summary: This set does belong, but only to the unsettled/wandering senses — te_aka:41515 ('to be unsettled, wandering, irresolute, uncertain'), williams:1928 ('Unsettled, wandering, irresolute'), and the hepatakakupu group whose Māori definition describes unsettled thought. It does NOT belong to the colour senses, the honorific 'Dame', or the rugby team.

findings.detail: Measured: 1,162 williams glosses are nothing but a cross-reference ('Cf. X', 'Variant of wahine.', 'Same as X', '= X') — 4.7% of its 24,976 senses. The other sources show 33 apparent hits and they are false positives ('See dimly', 'see you later, time will tell.'), so this is williams-specific. Crucially the data is NOT lost: 1,112 of the 1,162 already carry the cross-reference as a relation as well, so the gloss text is redundant rather than load-bearing, which makes it safe to stop writing it there. Checked for a spurious-merge hazard and found none: two 'Variant of X' glosses share only 'variant', giving coverage 0.33 against a high df, so they grade weak and do not merge each other.
findings.subject: williams gloss_en carrying cross-reference text
findings.summary: williams:1954's whole gloss is 'Cf. kaikaiarure.' — a pointer where the meaning should be. The sense therefore contributes nothing any evidence rule can match, and the source drops out of a three-way agreement it belongs in.

findings.detail: Recorded rather than diagnosed. The williams xref work deliberately refuses to guess a target when the spelling is ambiguous, so some UNRESOLVED is by design; what is not yet known is how much of the 1,112 is deliberate refusal versus unattempted. That measurement belongs with the fix, not here.
findings.subject: williams:1954 see_also -> kaikaiarure
findings.summary: The relation is recorded but UNRESOLVED — it names a headword it never resolved to an entry, so the pointer exists and connects nothing.
